claim: Experience-dependent modifications of synaptic connections are thought to change patterns of network activities and stimulus tuning with learning.
source: Experience-dependent modifications of synaptic connections are thought to change patterns of network activities and stimulus tuning with learning.
evidence: This is a general statement about the theoretical understanding in the field, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Only a few studies explored how synaptic plasticity shapes the response dynamics of cortical circuits.
source: However, only a few studies explored how synaptic plasticity shapes the response dynamics of cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, implying knowledge of existing research.

claim: Broadening the distribution of activities and stronger oscillations in the response dynamics after learning provide evidence for synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections modifying the strength of positive feedback.
source: Broadening the distribution of activities and stronger oscillations in the response dynamics after learning provide evidence for synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections modifying the strength of positive feedback.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and modeling presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1, 3, and 5.

claim: Interplay between synaptic plasticity and slow negative feedback via firing rate adaptation is critical in sharpening response dynamics.
source: Its interplay with slow negative feedback via firing rate adaptation is critical in sharpening response dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by mean-field analysis and network simulations shown in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Analysis of changes in temporal patterns enables disentangling recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity.
source: Analysis of changes in temporal patterns also enables us to disentangle recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity and provides a measure for the strengths of recurrent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the modeling and fitting procedures described in the Results section and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Human and monkeys process familiar stimuli with shorter response times and with less effort.
source: Human and monkeys have been reported to process familiar stimuli with shorter response times and with less effort (Greene and Rayner, 2001; Logothetis et al., 1995; Mruczek and Sheinberg, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sharpening of stimulus selectivity is achieved by broadening the distribution of activities as the stimulus becomes familiar.
source: The possible neural correlate for such behavior enhancement is the sharpening of stimulus selectivity that is achieved by broadening the distribution of activities as the stimulus becomes familiar (Freedman et al., 2006; Kobatake et al., 1998; Lim et al., 2015; McKee et al., 2013; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Temporal sharpening of neural responses with experience has been observed, which can increase the resolution of discriminating stimuli in time with learning.
source: Also, temporal sharpening of neural responses with experience has been observed, which can increase the resolution of discriminating stimuli in time with learning (Meyer et al., 2014; Recanzone et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Modifications of synaptic connections have been thought to be one of the basic mechanisms for learning.
source: Modifications of synaptic connections have been thought to be one of the basic mechanisms for learning.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus.

claim: A repeated encounter of a stimulus would elicit a particular activity pattern in the network, which in turn modifies synaptic connections depending on pre- and post-synaptic activities.
source: A repeated encounter of a stimulus would elicit a particular activity pattern in the network, which in turn modifies synaptic connections depending on pre- and post-synaptic activities.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on established principles of synaptic plasticity.

claim: Inferior temporal cortex (ITC) is important for visual object recognition.
source: To this end, we consider neural activities recorded in inferior temporal cortex (ITC) known to be important for visual object recognition (Miyashita, 1993; Tanaka, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in the response properties with learning have been reported in several experiments in ITC.
source: In ITC, changes in the response properties with learning have been reported in several experiments (Freedman et al., 2006; Li et al., 1993; Lim et al., 2015; Logothetis et al., 1995; McKee et al., 2013; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous experimental studies.

claim: The average over different visual stimuli of time-averaged responses decreases with familiarity in ITC.
source: The average over different visual stimuli of time-averaged responses decreases with familiarity, while the distribution of responses across visual stimuli broadens with learning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and cited studies.

claim: The distribution of responses across visual stimuli broadens with learning in ITC.
source: The average over different visual stimuli of time-averaged responses decreases with familiarity, while the distribution of responses across visual stimuli broadens with learning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and cited studies.

claim: Rapid successive presentation of familiar images, but not novel images, elicits strong periodic responses in ITC.
source: The dynamics of visual responses were also found to change with familiarity – in particular, rapid successive presentation of familiar images, but not novel images, elicits strong periodic responses (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: The average response to familiar stimuli was lower than that to novel stimuli with a rapid decrease of the response around 150 ms after the stimulus onset in putative excitatory neurons.
source: In both cases, the average response to familiar stimuli was lower than that to novel stimuli with a rapid decrease of the response around 150 ms after the stimulus onset in putative excitatory neurons (Figure 1A; Figure 5A,B for the dimming-detection task).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 5A,B.

claim: The response to the most preferred stimulus was found to increase for familiar stimuli with broadening of the distribution of time-averaged activities.
source: On the other hand, the response to the most preferred stimulus was found to increase for familiar stimuli with broadening of the distribution of time-averaged activities (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: A rebound of activity was observed around 230 ms after the stimulus onset in both the mean and maximal responses to familiar stimuli.
source: In both the mean and maximal responses to familiar stimuli, a rebound of activity was observed around 230 ms after the stimulus onset (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Responses to novel stimuli show slow decay after the transient rise.
source: This is distinctive from responses to novel stimuli showing slow decay after the transient rise.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Higher-rank familiar stimuli exhibit the stronger rebound in putative excitatory neurons.
source: It showed that the higher-rank familiar stimuli exhibit the stronger rebound in putative excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is only a weak dependence between the rank of stimuli and the magnitude of rebound activity in inhibitory neurons.
source: In contrast, there is only a weak dependence between the rank of stimuli and the magnitude of rebound activity in inhibitory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average response showed damped oscillation for familiar stimuli in the dimming detection task with longer stimulus presentation.
source: In the dimming detection task with longer stimulus presentation, the average response showed damped oscillation for familiar stimuli (Figure 5B; Freedman et al., 2006; McKee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous studies.

claim: The peak response for the second familiar stimulus is as strong as the one for the first stimulus in rapid successive presentation.
source: In another experiment where either two novel stimuli or two familiar stimuli were presented rapidly in sequence, the peak response for the second familiar stimulus is as strong as the one for the first stimulus, while the response to the novel stimulus is suppressed at the second peak (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: The response to the novel stimulus is suppressed at the second peak in rapid successive presentation.
source: In another experiment where either two novel stimuli or two familiar stimuli were presented rapidly in sequence, the peak response for the second familiar stimulus is as strong as the one for the first stimulus, while the response to the novel stimulus is suppressed at the second peak (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Only excitatory neurons with their most preferred stimuli exhibit strong oscillation after learning.
source: Note that although all three experiments suggest stronger oscillation after learning, its strength may vary depending on a sampling of neurons and stimuli as only excitatory neurons with their most preferred stimuli exhibit strong oscillation after learning (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The prominent effects of visual learning on responses of excitatory neurons are (i) reduction in average response, (ii) increase in maximum response, and (iii) stronger oscillations after learning.
source: In sum, the prominent effects of visual learning on responses of excitatory neurons are (i) reduction in average response, (ii) increase in maximum response, and (iii) stronger oscillations after learning.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: The dynamics of inhibitory neurons follow that of mean excitatory neurons, and do not contribute qualitative changes of response dynamics after learning.
source: Note that we focus on excitatory neurons only assuming that the dynamics of inhibitory neurons follow that of mean excitatory neurons, and do not contribute qualitative changes of response dynamics after learning.
evidence: This is an assumption made for modeling, justified by experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Input changes and the magnitude of rebound activity depend weakly on the post-synaptic firing rates in inhibitory neurons.
source: Such a simplification is based on the experimental observation that input changes and the magnitude of rebound activity depend weakly on the post-synaptic firing rates in inhibitory neurons (See Discussion for further justification).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Synaptic plasticity alone is not sufficient to explain stronger oscillatory responses after learning.
source: We now extend this framework and explore whether synaptic plasticity alone would be sufficient to explain stronger oscillatory responses after learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling and analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hebbian-type synaptic plasticity with a potentiation in high firing rates leads to an increase of the maximal response of excitatory neurons.
source: Hebbian-type synaptic plasticity with a potentiation in high firing rates leads to an increase of the maximal response of excitatory neurons, while overall depression leads to a decrease of the average network response of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overall depression in synaptic plasticity leads to a decrease of the average network response of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Hebbian-type synaptic plasticity with a potentiation in high firing rates leads to an increase of the maximal response of excitatory neurons, while overall depression leads to a decrease of the average network response of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: With synaptic plasticity derived from the time-averaged activities, response dynamics shows similar changes to the time-averaged responses but the temporal profile is similar before and after learning and does not show oscillations after learning.
source: With such synaptic plasticity derived from the time-averaged activities, response dynamics in Equation (1) shows similar changes to the time-averaged responses (Figure 2B,C). However, the temporal profile is similar before and after learning and does not show oscillations after learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Specific negative feedback such as firing rate adaptation is required for generating a damped oscillatory response after learning.
source: For generating a damped oscillatory response after learning, we found that specific negative feedback such as firing rate adaptation is required (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mean-field analysis and modeling shown in Figure 3.

claim: Hebbian-type synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections provides strong potentiation in the connections among high firing rate neurons, and thus, generates a cell assembly with stronger positive feedback after learning.
source: Hebbian-type synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections provides strong potentiation in the connections among high firing rate neurons, and thus, generates a cell assembly with stronger positive feedback after learning (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling framework illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Strong potentiation in recurrent connections leads to not only an increase in the response of the cell assembly but also the emergence of oscillation under the interplay with slow adaptation currents.
source: This leads to not only an increase in the response of this cell assembly but also the emergence of oscillation under the interplay with slow adaptation currents.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling framework and mean-field analysis.

claim: The strength of oscillation in the rest of the population may depend on the synaptic strengths from high firing rate neurons.
source: The strength of oscillation in the rest of the population may depend on the synaptic strengths from these high firing rate neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the modeling framework.

claim: Potentiation of recurrent inputs in high firing rate neurons provides strong positive feedback in m, while slow adaptation mechanisms represented by n variables provide negative feedback.
source: Thus, potentiation of recurrent inputs in high firing rate neurons provides strong positive feedback in m, while slow adaptation mechanisms represented by n variables provide negative feedback.
evidence: This is derived from the mean-field analysis described in the text.

claim: Qualitative changes of the response dynamics in the network should be mainly led by the dynamics of m and n with strong potentiation in high rate neurons.
source: As the variables m and n are only present in the dynamics after learning, qualitative changes of the response dynamics in the network should be mainly led by their dynamics with strong potentiation in high rate neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference from the mean-field analysis illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Strong potentiation and generation of damped oscillation in high rate neurons are consistent with the observation that the rebound is strongest in those neurons.
source: Such strong potentiation and generation of damped oscillation in high rate neurons are consistent with the observation that the rebound is strongest in those neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This connects the modeling results with experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The recurrent input from high rate neurons can lead to a damped oscillatory response in the rest of the population.
source: The recurrent input from high rate neurons can lead to a damped oscillatory response in the rest of the population (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling framework illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The strength of the damped oscillatory response is proportional to the strength of postsynaptic synaptic plasticity fR(ξi) in the case of linear dynamics.
source: The mean-field analysis shows that the strength of the damped oscillatory response is proportional to the strength of postsynaptic synaptic plasticity fR(ξi) in the case of linear dynamics.
evidence: This is derived from the mean-field analysis described in the text.

claim: If fR for neuron i is positive (negative) corresponding to potentiation (depression) in recurrent inputs, an oscillation in neuron i would be in phase (out of phase) with that of high rate neurons.
source: If fR for neuron i is positive (negative) corresponding to potentiation (depression) in recurrent inputs, an oscillation in neuron i would be in phase (out of phase) with that of high rate neurons.
evidence: This is derived from the mean-field analysis described in the text.

claim: Overall depression-dominant synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections would lead to out of phase oscillation in the mean and maximum response, inconsistent with the data.
source: Previously, we proposed Hebbian-type but overall depression-dominant synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections to minimally account for the decrease in time-averaged responses (Lim et al., 2015). However, this would lead to out of phase oscillation in the mean and maximum response, inconsistent with the data (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis compared with experimental data in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Potentiation-dominant synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections would increase overall synaptic input and cannot reproduce a decrease in average activities with learning.
source: However, potentiation-dominant synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections would increase overall synaptic input and cannot reproduce a decrease in average activities with learning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Reduction in average response requires changes in external inputs or other recurrent inputs such as suppression in other excitatory inputs or enhanced inhibition.
source: Instead, reduction in average response requires changes in external inputs or other recurrent inputs such as suppression in other excitatory inputs or enhanced inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Enhanced recurrent inhibition resulting from an increase in inhibitory activities after learning is inconsistent with the experimental observations showing a reduction in inhibitory firing rates across different stimuli.
source: Enhanced recurrent inhibition can result from an increase in inhibitory activities after learning or potentiated inhibitory connections onto excitatory neurons. The former is inconsistent with the experimental observations showing a reduction in inhibitory firing rates across different stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Potentiated inhibition with learning is less likely to account for a decrease of average excitatory activities because the effect of potentiated inhibition in the late phase is weaker than in the early phase while reduction of excitatory activities was observed in the late phase.
source: Also, potentiated inhibition with learning is less likely to account for a decrease of average excitatory activities - a temporal profile of inhibitory activities after learning shows a decrease of activity almost to the baseline in the late phase of the stimulus presentation (200–250 ms after the stimulus onset). This suggests that the effect of potentiated inhibition in the late phase is weaker than in the early phase while reduction of excitatory activities was observed in the late phase (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Depression in slow excitatory currents can lead to a decrease in excitatory activities in the late phase.
source: Another possibility is a depression in recurrent excitation through different types of synapses such as potentiation in fast AMPA-like currents and depression in slow NMDA-like currents. Depression in slow excitatory currents can lead to a decrease in excitatory activities in the late phase.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: Different regulation of AMPA and NMDA currents is inconsistent with the experimental observations showing maintenance of a constant NMDA-to-AMPA ratio under the changes of AMPA receptors induced chemically or by an STDP protocol.
source: However, different regulation of AMPA and NMDA currents is inconsistent with the experimental observations showing maintenance of a constant NMDA-to-AMPA ratio under the changes of AMPA receptors induced chemically or by an STDP protocol (Watt et al., 2000; Watt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: An example network with Hebbian learning rule in recurrent connections, uniform depression in the feedforward connection, and spike adaptation mechanisms reproduces the effects of visual learning qualitatively.
source: In Figure 4, an example network with Hebbian learning rule in recurrent connections, uniform depression in the feedforward connection, and spike adaptation mechanisms was shown to reproduce the effects of visual learning qualitatively.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 4.

claim: With learning, the average response decreases in particular in the late phase.
source: With learning, the average response decreases in particular in the late phase (Figure 4A), but maximal firing rates increased and oscillation becomes prominent especially in high rates (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Maximal firing rates increased and oscillation becomes prominent especially in high rates with learning.
source: With learning, the average response decreases in particular in the late phase (Figure 4A), but maximal firing rates increased and oscillation becomes prominent especially in high rates (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: In the successive presentation of two stimuli, the average response shows stronger oscillation after learning.
source: Also, in the successive presentation of two stimuli, the average response shows stronger oscillation after learning (Figure 4D), while the rank of individual neuronal activities changes when a new stimulus arrives (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The rank of individual neuronal activities changes when a new stimulus arrives.
source: Also, in the successive presentation of two stimuli, the average response shows stronger oscillation after learning (Figure 4D), while the rank of individual neuronal activities changes when a new stimulus arrives (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: With synaptic or neuronal nonlinearity, some conditions identified through mean field dynamics can be mitigated such as less dominant potentiation in recurrent inputs with learning.
source: Note that the mean field dynamics was derived under the assumption of linear dynamics. With synaptic or neuronal nonlinearity, some conditions identified through our mean field dynamics can be mitigated such as less dominant potentiation in recurrent inputs with learning (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A network simulation with example nonlinearity still shows that the core principles on the synaptic plasticity rule remain the same as strong potentiation in recurrent connections in high rate neurons, and average depression in feedforward inputs.
source: However, a network simulation with example nonlinearity still shows that the core principles on the synaptic plasticity rule remain the same as strong potentiation in recurrent connections in high rate neurons, and average depression in feedforward inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Network models implementing the conditions identified through mean-field equations reproduce the experimental observation.
source: In this section, we validate that network models implementing the conditions identified through mean-field equations indeed reproduce the experimental observation and allow us to infer the post-synaptic dependence of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Potentiation in high firing rate neurons, average potentiation of recurrent inputs and depression in feedforward inputs were found to mimic response to familiar stimuli.
source: Potentiation in high firing rate neurons, average potentiation of recurrent inputs and depression in feedforward inputs were found to mimic response to familiar stimuli (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fitting of mean-field dynamics to experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mean-field dynamics reproduces prominent features of response dynamics before and after learning, showing damped oscillation and a decrease in average response to familiar stimuli after its peak.
source: This mean-field dynamics reproduces prominent features of response dynamics before and after learning, showing damped oscillation and a decrease in average response to familiar stimuli after its peak (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When novel stimuli are repeatedly shown, the peak response to the second stimuli is smaller than the response to the first, due to a slow recovery from the adaptation current.
source: When novel stimuli are repeatedly shown, the peak response to the second stimuli is smaller than the response to the first, due to a slow recovery from the adaptation current.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For the serial presentation of familiar stimuli, the response to the first stimulus decays quickly and the response to the second stimulus is less affected by the adaptation current.
source: In contrast, for the serial presentation of familiar stimuli, the response to the first stimulus decays quickly and the response to the second stimulus is less affected by the adaptation current.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The overall response becomes more oscillatory for familiar stimuli compared to the one for novel stimuli in successive presentation.
source: Thus, the overall response becomes more oscillatory compared to the one for novel stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The average post-synaptic dependence of synaptic plasticity leads to potentiation in recurrent inputs and depression in feedforward inputs.
source: Consistent with the fitting of the mean-field dynamics to the data obtained in a dimming detection task, the average post-synaptic dependence of synaptic plasticity leads to potentiation in recurrent inputs and depression in feedforward inputs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The post-synaptic dependence in recurrent connections is an increasing function of the rank of stimuli, or equivalently, the post-synaptic activities.
source: Furthermore, the post-synaptic dependence in recurrent connections is an increasing function of the rank of stimuli, or equivalently, the post-synaptic activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated through fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dependence of the rebound magnitude to familiar stimuli on the rank of stimuli is similar to the post-synaptic dependence in recurrent connections.
source: It is notable that such a tendency is similar to the dependence of the rebound magnitude to familiar stimuli on the rank of stimuli observed experimentally (Figure 1D).
evidence: This connects the modeling results with experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Network models implementing the derived synaptic plasticity reproduce the reduction of average activities and rebound in the late phase of stimulus presentation in both average and maximal responses.
source: Network models implementing the derived synaptic plasticity reproduce the reduction of average activities (Figure 6B) and rebound in the late phase of stimulus presentation in both average and maximal responses, although the maximal response after the initial rise is less well fitted (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through network simulation shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Firing rate adaptation mechanisms are a good candidate for slow negative feedback to explain the familiarity effect on the dynamics.
source: Our mean field analysis and model fit to the data suggest firing rate adaptation mechanisms as a good candidate for slow negative feedback to explain the familiarity effect on the dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling and data fitting results.

claim: Delayed global inhibition may arise due to local inhibition with slow NMDA- or GABAB-like currents in inhibitory feedback pathways, or inhibitory feedback from other areas.
source: Delayed global inhibition may arise due to local inhibition with slow NMDA- or GABAB-like currents in inhibitory feedback pathways, or inhibitory feedback from other areas.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Prefrontal cortex shows a familiarity effect with a long latency around 100 ms but with opposite sign.
source: For instance, prefrontal cortex shows a familiarity effect with a long latency around 100 ms but with opposite sign (Rainer and Miller, 2000; Xiang and Brown, 2004), and thus, the top-down signals from this area can serve as slow negative feedback.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Top-down signals from prefrontal cortex can serve as slow negative feedback.
source: For instance, prefrontal cortex shows a familiarity effect with a long latency around 100 ms but with opposite sign (Rainer and Miller, 2000; Xiang and Brown, 2004), and thus, the top-down signals from this area can serve as slow negative feedback.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited observations.

claim: Without negative feedback, m cannot generate damped oscillations after learning in both high rate neurons and the overall population.
source: Without negative feedback, m cannot generate damped oscillations after learning in both high rate neurons and the overall population.
evidence: This is derived from the mean-field analysis of the global inhibition model.

claim: Slow negative feedback private to individual neurons or sub-populations is required to generate qualitative changes in dynamics as interacting with synaptic plasticity.
source: This suggests that slow negative feedback private to individual neurons or sub-populations is required to generate qualitative changes in dynamics as interacting with synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference from the mean-field analysis of the global inhibition model.

claim: Short-term depression in synaptic connections has been suggested as a mechanism for negative feedback and generating oscillations in cortical circuits.
source: Short-term depression in synaptic connections has also been suggested as a mechanism for negative feedback and generating oscillations in cortical circuits (Laing and Chow, 2002; Loebel and Tsodyks, 2002; Tabak et al., 2006; Wang, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A simple phenomenological model of short-term plasticity cannot explain the qualitative changes in response dynamics observed experimentally.
source: However, the network simulation with the best-fitted parameters cannot generate a strong rebound, unlike the adaptation mechanisms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). Thus, a simple phenomenological model of short-term plasticity cannot explain the qualitative changes in response dynamics observed experimentally.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The emergence of damped oscillations after learning requires strong positive feedback through potentiation in recurrent connections particularly among neurons with high firing rates.
source: The emergence of damped oscillations after learning requires strong positive feedback through potentiation in recurrent connections particularly among neurons with high firing rates.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the modeling and analysis.

claim: Recurrent synaptic plasticity broadens the distribution of activities, while depression in feedforward inputs decreases average firing rates.
source: Such recurrent synaptic plasticity broadens the distribution of activities, while depression in feedforward inputs decreases average firing rates.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the modeling and analysis.

claim: Synaptic plasticity enables the sparse and efficient representation of the learned stimuli.
source: Synaptic plasticity, therefore, enables the sparse and efficient representation of the learned stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The strength of rebound of damped oscillation observed after learning can be a novel, graded measure for recurrent synaptic plasticity.
source: Furthermore, the strength of rebound of damped oscillation observed after learning can be a novel, graded measure for recurrent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results and their connection to experimental observations.

claim: Adaptation-like mechanisms are critical for enhanced oscillatory responses after learning, and strongly suppresses the neural activities for the learned stimuli in particular in the late phase of the stimulus presentation.
source: On the other hand, adaptation-like mechanisms are critical for enhanced oscillatory responses after learning, and strongly suppresses the neural activities for the learned stimuli in particular in the late phase of the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the modeling and analysis.

claim: Temporal sharpening prepares neurons to respond to the subsequent stimulus.
source: As such temporal sharpening prepares neurons to respond to the subsequent stimulus, our work suggests that the adaptation mechanisms together with synaptic plasticity may play an important role in the rapid processing of the learned stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The adaptation mechanisms together with synaptic plasticity may play an important role in the rapid processing of the learned stimuli.
source: As such temporal sharpening prepares neurons to respond to the subsequent stimulus, our work suggests that the adaptation mechanisms together with synaptic plasticity may play an important role in the rapid processing of the learned stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the modeling results.

claim: Analyzing time-course data allows disentangling contributions of synaptic plasticity in different connections.
source: Analyzing time-course data allows disentangling contributions of synaptic plasticity in different connections.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the work.

claim: Only post-synaptic dependence of the synaptic plasticity rules can be inferred from single cell recordings under the assumption that the learning rules are a separable function of pre- and postsynaptic rates.
source: However, similar to the previous work, only post-synaptic dependence of the synaptic plasticity rules can be inferred from single cell recordings under the assumption that the learning rules are a separable function of pre- and postsynaptic rates.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the inference method.

claim: There is a strong correlation between neural activity and the threshold separating depression and potentiation, but no correlation when the post-synaptic activity is normalized.
source: On the other hand, time-averaged data allows to infer recurrent synaptic plasticity in different neurons, which reveals a strong correlation between neural activity and the threshold separating depression and potentiation, but no correlation when the post-synaptic activity is normalized (Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The relatively small variance of rebound strengths over neurons may support the assumption that synaptic plasticity rules are the same across different neurons when inputs and rates are normalized.
source: Although a direct test of this assumption is not feasible, the relatively small variance of rebound strengths over neurons may support this assumption on the recurrent synaptic plasticity as the dependence of rebound strengths on the rank of stimuli alternatively represents learning rules in recurrent connections (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Depression in the feedforward connections required to lower average response after learning reasserts the role of feedforward synaptic plasticity suggested for familiarity detection.
source: Depression in the feedforward connections required to lower average response after learning reasserts the role of feedforward synaptic plasticity suggested for familiarity detection (Bogacz and Brown, 2003; Norman and O'Reilly, 2003; Sohal and Hasselmo, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the modeling results.

claim: Most theoretical works implementing synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections have focused on associative memory and the emergence of attractors with learning.
source: On the other hand, most theoretical works implementing synaptic plasticity in recurrent connections have focused on associative memory and the emergence of attractors with learning (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Pereira and Brunel, 2018; Sohal and Hasselmo, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity are required to reproduce changes in spatial and temporal patterns underlying familiarity detection.
source: Unlike most of the previous works focusing on one-type of synaptic plasticity, our analysis proposed that both recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity are required to reproduce changes in spatial and temporal patterns underlying familiarity detection.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the modeling and analysis.

claim: Firing rate adaptation mechanisms have been suggested to be critical in generating network oscillations and synchrony.
source: As a substrate for slow negative feedback, firing rate adaptation mechanisms have been suggested to be critical in generating network oscillations and synchrony (Ermentrout et al., 2001; Fuhrmann et al., 2002; La Camera et al., 2004; Laing and Chow, 2002; Tabak et al., 2006; van Vreeswijk and Hansel, 2001; Wang, 2010), and in optimal information transmission under a particular form of synaptic plasticity (Hennequin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Firing rate adaptation mechanisms have been suggested to be critical in optimal information transmission under a particular form of synaptic plasticity.
source: As a substrate for slow negative feedback, firing rate adaptation mechanisms have been suggested to be critical in generating network oscillations and synchrony (Ermentrout et al., 2001; Fuhrmann et al., 2002; La Camera et al., 2004; Laing and Chow, 2002; Tabak et al., 2006; van Vreeswijk and Hansel, 2001; Wang, 2010), and in optimal information transmission under a particular form of synaptic plasticity (Hennequin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effect of synaptic plasticity on enhancing synchrony in the recurrent synaptic circuits has been explored theoretically.
source: The effect of synaptic plasticity on enhancing synchrony in the recurrent synaptic circuits also has been explored theoretically (Gilson et al., 2010; Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2002; Morrison et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interplay between synaptic plasticity and adaptation with the time constant consistent with that of cellular adaptation mechanisms generate synchronous damped oscillations after learning.
source: Consistent with these previous works, our work suggests that the interplay between synaptic plasticity and adaptation with the time constant consistent with that of cellular adaptation mechanisms (Benda and Herz, 2003) generate synchronous damped oscillations after learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the modeling and analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The adaptation mechanisms in the temporal cortex have been suggested to encode the recency of stimuli, which is typically measured by suppression of the response to the repetition of a stimulus.
source: Previously, the adaptation mechanisms in the temporal cortex have been suggested to encode the recency of stimuli, which is typically measured by suppression of the response to the repetition of a stimulus (Meyer and Rust, 2018; Miller et al., 1991; Vogels, 2016; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The time scale of repetition suppression lasts up to seconds and may require the adaptation mechanisms on the much longer time scale.
source: As the time scale of repetition suppression lasts up to seconds, it may require the adaptation mechanisms on the much longer time scale (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation.

claim: Adaptation on various time scales may be required for different types of recognition memory.
source: Thus, adaptation on various time scales (La Camera et al., 2006; Pozzorini et al., 2013) may be required for different types of recognition memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: No dependence of input changes on post-synaptic firing rates in inhibitory neurons suggests that changes in inhibitory activities with learning can reflect the reduction of average excitatory activities without synaptic plasticity in the excitatory-to-inhibitory connections.
source: First, no dependence of input changes on post-synaptic firing rates in inhibitory neurons observed experimentally suggests that changes in inhibitory activities with learning can reflect the reduction of average excitatory activities and thereafter, excitatory inputs to inhibitory neurons without synaptic plasticity in the excitatory (E)-to-inhibitory (I) connections (Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations cited.

claim: Anti-Hebbian synaptic plasticity in the I-to-E connections can have similar effects as Hebbian-synaptic plasticity in the E-to-E connections.
source: On the other hand, anti-Hebbian synaptic plasticity in the I-to-E connections can have similar effects as Hebbian-synaptic plasticity in the E-to-E connections.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Overall potentiation in the I-to-E connections can provide stronger negative feedback or can replace the role of feedforward synaptic plasticity.
source: Alternatively, overall potentiation in the I-to-E connections can provide stronger negative feedback or can replace the role of feedforward synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The dynamics of inhibitory neurons show strong suppression almost to the baseline in the late phase of the stimulus presentation after learning.
source: However, as the dynamics of inhibitory neurons show strong suppression almost to the baseline in the late phase of the stimulus presentation after learning (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), neither anti-Hebbian synaptic plasticity nor potentiation can account for an increase of maximal response of excitatory neurons in the early phase and overall reduction in activities in the late phase (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in the inhibitory pathway are less likely to induce oscillation or suppression in the excitatory neurons.
source: Thus, we assumed that changes in the inhibitory pathway are less likely to induce oscillation or suppression in the excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and modeling considerations.

claim: The interaction between synaptic plasticity in both recurrent excitatory and inhibitory connections was suggested to reproduce increased transient response with learning.
source: It is notable that the interaction between synaptic plasticity in both recurrent excitatory and inhibitory connections was suggested to reproduce increased transient response with learning (Moldakarimov et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The homeostatic inhibitory plasticity proposed in previous work cannot reproduce damped oscillatory response observed in ITC.
source: Although the homeostatic inhibitory plasticity proposed in this work cannot reproduce damped oscillatory response observed in ITC, we cannot rule out the role of inhibitory synaptic plasticity that can be complementary to the mechanisms proposed in our work.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: The enhanced oscillation for familiar stimuli investigated here was around 5 Hz, which is in the range of theta oscillations.
source: The enhanced oscillation for familiar stimuli investigated here was around 5 Hz, which is in the range of theta oscillations.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the experimental data and modeling results.

claim: Low-frequency oscillation has been discussed in visual search to characterize overt exploration or sampling behaviors such as saccadic or microsaccadic eye movements.
source: Such a low-frequency oscillation has been discussed in visual search to characterize overt exploration or sampling behaviors such as saccadic or microsaccadic eye movements (Otero-Millan et al., 2008; Buzsaki, 2011) and to underlie covert shift of attention that samples different stimuli rhythmically (Dugué et al., 2015; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low-frequency oscillation underlies covert shift of attention that samples different stimuli rhythmically.
source: Such a low-frequency oscillation has been discussed in visual search to characterize overt exploration or sampling behaviors such as saccadic or microsaccadic eye movements (Otero-Millan et al., 2008; Buzsaki, 2011) and to underlie covert shift of attention that samples different stimuli rhythmically (Dugué et al., 2015; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rollenhagen and Olson (2005) observed that low-frequency oscillation became stronger when another stimulus was present together.
source: In line with these studies, Rollenhagen and Olson (2005) observed that low-frequency oscillation became stronger when another stimulus was present together.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Competitive interactions between populations representing different stimuli were suggested to generate oscillation with fatigue mechanism.
source: Competitive interactions between populations representing different stimuli were suggested to generate oscillation with fatigue mechanism (Moldakarimov et al., 2005; Rollenhagen and Olson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Competition between two different familiar stimuli can generate stronger oscillation at a similar frequency based on the adaptation mechanisms proposed in the current work.
source: Based on the adaptation mechanisms proposed in the current work, competition between two different familiar stimuli can generate stronger oscillation at a similar frequency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stronger oscillation but with the similar frequency with that for the single stimulus presentation was reproduced in the presentation of two stimuli in the mean-field dynamics with two mutually inhibitory populations.
source: In the mean-field dynamics with two mutually inhibitory populations each of which mimics the maximum response to a single familiar stimulus, stronger oscillation but with the similar frequency with that for the single stimulus presentation was reproduced in the presentation of two stimuli (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling shown in Figure 7.

claim: Low-frequency damped oscillators for a single familiar stimulus can be a building block for a rhythmic sampling of multiple stimuli and covert attentional shift through competitive interactions.
source: This may indicate low-frequency damped oscillators for a single familiar stimulus can be a building block for a rhythmic sampling of multiple stimuli and covert attentional shift through competitive interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the modeling results.

claim: Additional analysis of response dynamics revealed the role of slow adaptation currents in shaping response dynamics.
source: As an extension of our previous work that inferred the synaptic plasticity rules from changes in spatial patterns, additional analysis of response dynamics revealed the role of slow adaptation currents in shaping response dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution of the work.

claim: Different contributions to activity changes of recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity can be utilized to examine how each synaptic plasticity engages during the progress of learning.
source: Different contributions to activity changes of recurrent and feedforward synaptic plasticity suggested in our work can be further utilized to examine how each synaptic plasticity engages during the progress of learning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Interactions between ITC and perirhinal cortex may form positive feedback given the adjacency of these two areas and similar familiarity effects observed experimentally.
source: Also, although we suggested a local circuit model for visual learning, interactions with other areas might also be important – for instance, the interactions between ITC and perirhinal cortex may form positive feedback given the adjacency of these two areas and similar familiarity effects observed experimentally (Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation.

claim: Prefrontal cortex showing opposite effects of familiarity with a long latency may provide slow negative feedback.
source: On the other hand, prefrontal cortex showing opposite effects of familiarity with a long latency may provide slow negative feedback (Xiang and Brown, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation.
